extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, junior faculty, and practicing mathematicians (academic)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical professional duties and career-management advice for mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, junior faculty, and department chairs), covering service, teaching, advising, translation, interactions with administration, and career choices including industry. The page provides norms, cautions, and concrete recommendations for handling common professional situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide public and professional advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Your position as a Professor makes you a sort of cultural icon and you could be asked advice by almost anyone about almost anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to serve the public and campus community (examples: ballot design, probability questions for legal cases, police reports, map-area calculations). Treat such requests as recreational and service activities that help the profession and community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership in professional societies
rubrics_metrics.description: You, a budding mathematician, should belong to one or more of the professional societies (AMS, MAA, SIAM, AWM, NAM, SACNAS, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership is relatively inexpensive (about $160 per annum; AMS dues reduced for early years) and brings benefits: conferences, book series, journals, MathSciNet, networking, periodicals to keep up with developments, and infrastructure support. Societies are vital to the profession and to individual careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve as a translator for mathematical works
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators provide an important service: translating articles and books (especially from Russian, Chinese, Japanese, etc.) into English so others can read them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on automatic online translators for mathematics—they are poor for technical language. Publishers typically want a Ph.D. mathematician because translations must render sense precisely (definitions, negative statements, proofs). Translation is valuable professionally but often poorly paid and is frequently done as a service to the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand economics and remuneration of translation work
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing budgets for advanced math books and journal translations are slim; translators are paid modestly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect limited pay (e.g., AMS ≈ $20/page for journal translation; some publishers pay per line). Translation is often done for professional service rather than lucrative compensation; assess whether you want to do it primarily for service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize mathematics' dual role (service department and research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is often seen administratively as a 'service department' (teaching calculus to many non-majors) while simultaneously being a center of serious research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to explain and defend the department's multiple roles: high undergraduate teaching loads, contributions to other disciplines, research activity, grant activity, and service. Use data about teaching hours, majors, and curricular innovations to communicate value to administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and advocate department value to administration
rubrics_metrics.description: When meeting with Deans, Chairs must convey the Department's contributions—teaching workload, curriculum, research, and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on excuses; provide concrete statistics and examples to justify the department's priorities. Be ready to counter simplistic comparisons (e.g., teaching evaluations) and to demonstrate strengths in teaching, research, and cross-disciplinary cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage a sequence of 1-year jobs strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: A string of 1-year, non-renewable positions can be chaotic and destructive to research productivity and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on time and career-management: secure chunks of research time and produce items for your CV, avoid overcommitting to committees or time drains, gear your life toward the next job search. Consider industry or government positions as non-permanent alternatives that can provide stability, pay, and a path back to academe if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine your role when you cannot get along with a colleague
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot get along with a mentor, supervisor, or Chair, first determine whether the problem is at least partly your fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are at fault, fix the situation. If not, explore options: find another mentor, cultivate relationships with others, avoid toxic supervisors where possible, or accept the situation temporarily. Maintain a good relationship with your Chair where possible because the Chair influences tenure, raises, and assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve departmental disputes constructively
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous disagreement is healthy, but protracted conflict damages collegiality and departmental function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for robust debate that ends with mutual respect and the ability to work together; seek reconciliation and common ground. If disputes escalate, seek appropriate institutional resources (e.g., mediation), recognizing the Dean might not always be a neutral party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond professionally to contentious teaching-reform debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching reform movements (e.g., 'the lecture is dead') can polarize departments, especially when large grants reward reform projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize legitimate differences, avoid personalizing disputes over pedagogy, and understand that grant-funded reforms can offer valuable resources and high-profile contributions to departmental teaching. Integrate collaborators and reformers constructively into departmental teaching missions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage relations with undergraduate students empathetically
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot get along with undergraduates, it is likely your fault; undergraduates are usually willing and pleasant learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt tolerance and understanding of student perspectives; vary teaching style (guest instructors, films, discussions) to re-engage a disengaged class; be interactive; use mid-term anonymous evaluations; speak with students to diagnose and fix problems; avoid overly authoritarian first-day rules that set a negative tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require/encourage TA teaching training
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing mandatory teaching methodology training for graduate student TAs improves teaching quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instituting a formal course before TAs teach (e.g., a three-credit-hour semester-long course) helps ensure teaching readiness and signals departmental seriousness about teaching. Chairs and senior faculty can participate to emphasize importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet Ph.D. students before accepting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept a Ph.D. student 'cold'—a Ph.D. relationship is a long-term, intensive commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get to know prospective students through classes, reading courses, oral presentations, and mentoring interactions to learn work habits, personality, and communication. Use these mechanisms to judge whether a long-term advising partnership will work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deal proactively with problematic graduate students
rubrics_metrics.description: If a graduate student becomes blocked, disruptive, mentally unstable, or otherwise problematic, do not handle it alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use campus psychiatrists/counselors, consult experienced colleagues, consider helping the student obtain a terminal Master's degree if appropriate, and involve departmental/institutional resources. Prioritize safety and seek help for threatening behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider industry careers a valid and often attractive alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitioning to industry is not a failure; industry offers diverse opportunities (actuarial work, genome projects, NSA, finance, software, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry typically provides higher pay, more frequent raises and promotions, and work that is results-oriented and often directly used by others. Evaluate industry roles on their own merits—work will be constrained by company needs but can be professionally satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand differences in career reward structures (academia vs. industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic career progression (notably two big promotions) differs from industry progression (more frequent raises and promotions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage expectations: in academia, promotions and raises may be infrequent and tied to tenure/promotion events; in industry, compensation and promotion opportunities can be more regular. Factor this into career decisions and life planning.
